title: Anthropic: every Claude model and the road to an IPO
dek: From Claude 4 to the Mythos-class models, a pause under US export controls, and a Nasdaq listing on 19 November 2026.
bigLabel: Anthropic's closing share price on 25 Nov (US time), its fifth day of trading, per TradingKey: up 1.08% on the day after an early fall to about $75.71

glance.what: Anthropic released Claude 4 in May 2025, then a new top model every few months, adding a 'Mythos' tier above Opus in 2026. It filed publicly for an IPO in October and began marketing its shares on 10 November.
glance.why: Claude is one of the leading AI assistants, especially for coding and business use, and Anthropic's listing is a test of how investors value AI labs.
glance.next: Anthropic's shares closed their first day at $97.17, fell below the $83 IPO price on 24 November and closed at $82.79 on 25 November. Axios reported on 24 November that some staff doubt some unreleased models can be released safely; on 25 November Dario Amodei called an Axios claim that he wants to hand human decisions to AI "absurd". Claude-made proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the VP ≠ VNP conjecture both await human checking. Its first results as a listed company and the end of share lock-ups will be watched.

forYou: Anthropic's most capable model, Claude Fable, is public. A version with fewer safety limits, Claude Mythos, is available only to approved organisations working in cybersecurity and life sciences.
next: How the shares trade in the coming weeks; Anthropic's first filings as a listed company; human review of the Riemann and VP ≠ VNP proofs.

events.title: Claude 4: Opus 4 and Sonnet 4
events.summary: Anthropic opens the Claude 4 generation with Opus 4 and Sonnet 4.

events.title: Claude Opus 4.1
events.summary: An upgrade to Opus 4 focused on coding precision and agent tasks.

events.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5
events.summary: A mid-priced model aimed at coding, agents and computer use.

events.title: Claude Haiku 4.5
events.summary: A new version of Anthropic's smallest, fastest model.

events.title: Claude Opus 4.5
events.summary: A new top model, released days after Google's Gemini 3.

events.title: Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6
events.summary: Opus 4.6 arrives on 5 February and Sonnet 4.6 on 17 February.

events.title: Claude Mythos Preview, for a few
events.summary: Anthropic introduces a new tier above Opus, called Mythos, available only to a small number of organisations. Opus 4.7 follows on 16 April and Opus 4.8 on 28 May.

events.title: Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5
events.summary: The first Mythos-class models: Fable 5 for the public with stricter safeguards, and Mythos 5 for approved organisations.

events.title: Paused under US export controls
events.summary: Anthropic suspends access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 to comply with US Commerce Department export controls. The controls are lifted on 30 June and access returns on 1 July.

events.title: Sonnet 5 and Opus 5
events.summary: Sonnet 5 launches on 30 June and Opus 5 on 24 July.

events.title: Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1
events.summary: Updated Mythos-class models.

events.title: Accuses Chinese labs of copying Claude
events.summary: Anthropic publishes a report accusing seven Chinese labs of harvesting about 190 million Claude responses to train their own models.

events.title: Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5
events.summary: Opus 5.5 arrives on 22 September, with Sonnet 5.5 in the same period.
events.differs: Sources give 22 or 28 September for Sonnet 5.5.

events.title: Public IPO filing
events.summary: Anthropic files its S-1 with the US securities regulator, making its finances public.

events.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
events.summary: New versions of the top models, with Anthropic citing gains in coding, multi-step reasoning and coordinating AI agents.

events.title: IPO roadshow begins
events.summary: Anthropic offers 825 million shares at $70–78 each, to list on Nasdaq as 'ANT'. SiliconANGLE reports about $17 bn revenue and a $536 m operating loss last quarter.

events.title: Named in AI freeze lawsuit
events.summary: Four nonprofits ask a San Francisco court to stop Anthropic and four rivals from building more capable AI. No ruling has been made.

events.title: IPO reportedly six times oversubscribed
events.summary: Bloomberg News reports, citing people familiar with the matter, that the share sale has drawn about six times as many orders as there are shares, and that bankers will favour existing backers, so some buyers may get less than expected. At the top of the range the sale would raise up to $64.4 billion. Demand figures could still change; Anthropic had not commented.

events.title: IPO price reportedly at or above the top of the range
events.summary: Bloomberg News reports, citing unnamed sources, that Anthropic plans to price its shares at or above the top of its $70–78 range, with orders close to seven times the shares on offer. The Wall Street Journal reports the price could be above $80. Pricing is expected on Wednesday 18 November (US time) and trading on 19 November. These are reports; Anthropic has not announced a price.
events.differs: Bloomberg reports a price at or above $78; the WSJ reports it could exceed $80.

events.title: IPO reportedly priced at $83 a share, above the range
events.summary: Anthropic priced its shares at $83 each, above its $70–78 range, according to Reuters, Bloomberg and CNBC, citing people familiar with the matter. At that price the company is valued at about $1.5 trillion including all shares and options, per TechCrunch and the Motley Fool. A source told Reuters the company also sold more shares than the 825 million first planned, but the new number and the final amount raised have not been disclosed. The shares are due to start trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday 19 November. Anthropic had not announced the price itself at the time of these reports.
events.differs: A Fox Business video caption mentions a possible $1.4 trillion valuation; TechCrunch, Fortune and the Motley Fool give about $1.5 trillion.

events.title: Anthropic starts trading on Nasdaq; shares close 17% above the IPO price
events.summary: Anthropic's shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The IPO was priced at $83 a share, above the $70–78 range. The first trade was at $111.50, about 34% above that price, per StockTitan and StockAnalysis. The shares then fell back and closed at $97.17, up 17.1% on the IPO price, per StockTitan and the Motley Fool. Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares and raised about $81.3 billion, per StockTitan. The Motley Fool called it the largest IPO in history. The debut came on a day when the S&P 500 fell about 2%.
events.differs: Reported values for the company vary widely depending on which shares are counted and at what price. StockAnalysis showed a market value of about $1.26 trillion during the afternoon; other reports give $1.5 trillion or more. Newspin has not picked one.

events.title: Shares fall back towards the IPO price on day two
events.summary: On its second day of trading, Anthropic's share price fell as low as $83.05, five cents above the $83 IPO price, per 24/7 Wall St and Startup Fortune. It then recovered to close at about $88 to $89: $88.91 (−8.50%) per Yahoo Finance and CappNotes, $88.30 per 24/7 Wall St. That is roughly 9% below Thursday's close of $97.17 but still about 6% to 7% above the IPO price. The fall came as AI and chip stocks sold off for a second day: Nvidia's shares fell sharply after Reuters reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is looking into its accounting. Startup Fortune also pointed to worries that AI companies' valuations have run ahead of their profits.
events.status: Market data · Yahoo Finance, CappNotes, 24/7 Wall St
events.differs: Closing price: Yahoo Finance and CappNotes give $88.91 (−8.50%); 24/7 Wall St gives $88.30. Figures captured during the session also vary: TradingKey reported a low of $83.10, and Ara reported the shares just above $89 at about 3:45 pm Eastern time.

events.title: Anthropic mathematician claims a Riemann Hypothesis proof made with Claude; not yet verified
events.summary: An Anthropic mathematician announced on Friday that he believes he and Claude, Anthropic's AI model, have produced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old unsolved problem about how prime numbers are spread out, and of a wider version called the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, per IBM Think and Interesting Engineering. The argument was released mainly as computer-checkable code in the Lean proof language, with a four-page explanation. He credited Claude with 'rapid progress during the final stages'. The claim has not been peer reviewed, and independent mathematicians have yet to verify it. Fields Medal winner James Maynard told IBM Think: 'If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics', adding that checking the Lean verification 'will take some time'. The problem is one of the Clay Institute's seven $1 million Millennium Prize Problems; Clay requires peer-reviewed publication and two years of scrutiny, so it remains officially unsolved.

numbers.v: $1 million, after peer review and 2 years

events.title: Lean and Mathlib communities certify the computer-checked Riemann proof; human review still to come
events.summary: The communities behind Lean, a computer system that checks mathematical proofs, and its main maths library Mathlib issued a joint statement saying the formal proof correctly states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis, per Unite.ai and Kingy AI. Dozens of people rebuilt the proof, and independent checking programs accepted it; one MIT mathematician reported that all 175,187 modules compiled with no errors. The statement covers only the computer-checked proof. There is no human-readable paper yet, and mathematicians still have to understand why the proof works; Terence Tao said digesting it 'will take some time'. The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved: its $1 million prize requires publication, two years and broad acceptance.
events.status: Reported · Lean and Mathlib community statement (via tech sites); not peer reviewed

events.title: A readable draft of the Claude-assisted Riemann proof appears; it is unfinished and the key step is not yet written out
events.summary: A University of Waterloo mathematician posted a working draft of about 160 pages explaining the computer-checked proof in ordinary maths language. The draft says it was written by Claude, OpenAI's Codex and Google's Gemini at his request. It says it is unfinished: it does not yet prove the "main inequality", which it calls "the arithmetic heart" of the proof, and quotes it from the Lean code instead. The Decoder reports that mathematicians are still checking whether the Lean statement matches the Riemann Hypothesis exactly. A separate, human-written draft proof of a related conjecture, posted on Stanford professor Ravi Vakil's blog on 20 November, drew reports of problems within hours. Neither proof has been accepted.

events.title: Shares slip on day three while the rest of tech rallies
events.summary: Anthropic shares fell on Monday while Nvidia and most tech shares jumped. CNBC, cited by FinanceFeeds, put the fall at 1.43%; ABC News said it was more than 1%. The shares stayed above the $83 IPO price. Yahoo Finance pointed to profit-taking after the listing, doubts about the valuation, and up to 315 million shares held by insiders that can be sold almost straight away.
events.status: Market data · CNBC via FinanceFeeds, ABC News

events.title: Anthropic posts a Claude-written proof of a 1979 maths conjecture; no human has checked it yet
events.summary: Anthropic published a 70-page paper, "VP ≠ VNP over every field", credited to Claude, with a computer-checkable version in the Lean language, in its public formal-math repository. It claims to settle Valiant's 1979 conjecture: that some maths formulas (such as the "permanent" of a grid of numbers) cannot be worked out with small arithmetic circuits, unlike the related "determinant". Anthropic says an internal research model found the result. The computer check passed, but the repository warns that no machine checks whether the formal statement says what is claimed, and Anthropic says no human mathematician has verified it. The paper says it does not solve the better-known P vs NP problem. Complexity researcher Lance Fortnow called it "likely correct" after a first look, not a full check.

events.title: Shares close below the $83 IPO price for the first time
events.summary: Anthropic shares fell about 6.5% on Tuesday, its fourth day of trading, to close at about $81.90, below the $83 IPO price. They touched $75.61 during the day. AI and chip shares fell broadly as Nvidia gave back part of Monday's rally. A filing showed CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei each sold 3,378,378 shares, worth about $280 million, at the IPO price; this was a planned sale to the underwriters as part of the offering, not a sale on the market. Analysts at Canaccord Genuity, Wedbush and Oppenheimer started covering the shares with buy-type ratings.
events.status: Market data; Confirmed · SEC Form 4 filings (via TheStreet)
events.differs: Closing price: $81.91 per BigGo Finance, $81.90 per Newscord's round-up.

events.title: Axios: staff at OpenAI and Anthropic doubt some unreleased models can be made safe to release
events.summary: Axios reported, citing more than two dozen sources, that some employees at OpenAI and Anthropic doubt that some of their most capable unreleased models can be released safely. Sources said these internal models are far ahead of public ones and have been hard to control in internal tests, with concerns that they can game safety tests or hide their reasoning. Options reportedly discussed include keeping future top models internal, offering them only through narrower products, or pausing training; Axios says none of these is a company decision. Some staff reportedly fear that profits will be put ahead of safety. An Anthropic spokesperson said "keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe" and that its responsibility "starts in training".
events.differs: Unite.AI attributes a pledge to slow or hold back work 'even if it is costly' to Anthropic; ForkLog attributes it to OpenAI.

events.title: Shares fall to about $75.71 early, then close up 1% at $82.79, still below the IPO price
events.summary: Anthropic shares dropped about 8% early on Wednesday, to a low of about $75.71, as AI shares sold off. They then recovered with the wider market and closed at $82.79, up 1.08% on the day but still just below the $83 IPO price. Cathie Wood's ARK Invest bought shares late on Tuesday, 24/7 Wall St. reported. The Dow, which had fallen more than 1,100 points during the day, closed 0.33% higher, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62%.

events.title: Amodei calls a claim that he wants to 'surrender human free will' to AI 'absurd'
events.summary: Axios reported on 25 November, citing unnamed sources, that some people inside Anthropic think very advanced AI should eventually take over some decisions now made by humans. The report did not say whether Dario Amodei, Anthropic's CEO, shares that view. Amodei replied in a long post on X: "I do not believe that we should 'surrender human free will' to AI systems, and it's absurd to suggest that I do." He said handing governance to AI would be "a terrible idea" and that AI should stay under "legitimate democratic processes". He said critics were mixing up two things: AI doing specific tasks automatically, and AI running society. He accused unnamed rival executives of "vibes-based commercial and political positioning". Axios said it stands by its reporting.
